key_terms.meaning: For ay″+by′+cy=0, put y=e<sup>mx</sup>; the ODE becomes am²+bm+c=0.
Real distinct roots give C₁e<sup>m₁x</sup>+C₂e<sup>m₂x</sup>; repeated and complex roots give adjusted C.F. forms.
The general solution of the homogeneous equation, carrying arbitrary constants C₁, C₂, … .
Any one solution of the nonhomogeneous equation; it has no arbitrary constants.
For P(D)y=e<sup>ax</sup>V(x), a P.I. is e<sup>ax</sup>[1/P(D+a)]V(x); if P(a)≠0 and V=1, it is e<sup>ax</sup>/P(a).
If the right-hand side duplicates a C.F. term, multiply the trial P.I. by x<sup>s</sup>, where s is the multiplicity of that root.
W(y₁,y₂)=det[[y₁,y₂],[y₁′,y₂′]]=y₁y₂′−y₂y₁′.
Functions are independent when c₁y₁+c₂y₂+…+cₙyₙ=0 identically forces c₁=c₂=…=cₙ=0.
n linearly independent solutions of an nth-order homogeneous linear ODE.
Choose a trial y<sub>p</sub> with unknown constants shaped like the right-hand side, then substitute and compare coefficients.
The guessed form for y<sub>p</sub>; multiply by x<sup>s</sup> if it duplicates a term already in the C.F.
Replace constants in the C.F. by functions u₁(x), u₂(x), impose u₁′y₁+u₂′y₂=0, and integrate.

key_terms.term: Wronskian formula for variation of parameters
key_terms.meaning: For y″+p(x)y′+q(x)y=f(x), u₁′=−y₂f/W and u₂′=y₁f/W.
An equation ax²y″+bxy′+cy=f(x); the substitution x=e<sup>t</sup> gives constant coefficients.
An equation a(px+q)²y″+b(px+q)y′+cy=f(x); the substitution px+q=e<sup>t</sup> gives constant coefficients.
Two or more coupled linear equations in one independent variable; eliminate variables to get one higher-order equation.
If y₁ solves a variable-coefficient homogeneous ODE, y₂=y₁∫e<sup>−∫p dx</sup>/y₁² dx gives a second independent solution.
A system x′=P(x,y), y′=Q(x,y) with no explicit dependence on t.
A point where P(x,y)=0 and Q(x,y)=0; it is an equilibrium of the autonomous system.
At a critical point, Jacobian eigenvalues with negative real parts mean stability, positive real parts mean instability, pure imaginary means a centre.

takeaways: A constant-coefficient linear ODE turns into polynomial algebra through y=e<sup>mx</sup>.
The general solution is C.F. plus any one particular integral.
For simple right-hand sides, the P.I. shape copies the right-hand side unless it clashes with the C.F.
The Wronskian is the quick test for independence of solutions.
Undetermined coefficients is fast but needs constant coefficients and a special right-hand side.
Variation of parameters works for variable coefficients once two independent homogeneous solutions are known.
A Cauchy-Euler equation becomes constant-coefficient under x=e<sup>t</sup>.
Coupled constant-coefficient ODEs can be eliminated into one higher-order ODE.
One known solution of a second-order variable-coefficient ODE gives the second by reduction of order.
Phase-plane critical points are classified by the eigenvalues of the Jacobian.
bank_note: Long answers usually demand full C.F. and P.I. work, a Wronskian independence test, variation-of-parameters integrals, Cauchy-Euler substitution, and phase-plane stability classification.

bank.q: State the superposition principle for linear homogeneous ODEs and explain how independent solutions build the complementary function.
outline: Superposition: linear combinations of solutions are solutions.

bank.q: Write the characteristic equation of ay″+by′+cy=0 and list the three C.F. forms for distinct real, repeated, and complex roots.
outline: Complex roots α±iβ: e<sup>αx</sup>(C₁cos βx+C₂sin βx).

bank.q: Define the Wronskian of two functions and state the theorem linking a nonzero Wronskian to linear independence of solutions.
outline: Nonzero W on an interval implies independence for solutions.
Zero W can indicate dependence for solutions of a linear ODE.

bank.q: Explain the method of undetermined coefficients and state when the trial solution must be multiplied by x or x².
outline: Trial form matches the right-hand side.
Multiply by x<sup>s</sup> when the trial duplicates a C.F. term; s is the multiplicity.

bank.q: Solve y″−5y′+6y=e<sup>3x</sup>+x². Find C.F., P.I., and the general solution; handle the resonance in e<sup>3x</sup>.
outline: For e<sup>3x</sup>, use Axe<sup>3x</sup> and get A=1.
For x², use Ax²+Bx+C and solve constants.
Add C.F. and both P.I. parts.

bank.q: Solve y″+4y=sin 2x by undetermined coefficients, noting the resonance with the complementary function.
outline: Substitute and compare; result y<sub>p</sub>=−x cos 2x/4.

bank.q: Solve the Cauchy-Euler equation x²y″−3xy′+4y=0 for x>0.
Use variation of parameters to solve y″+y=sec x.
outline: Homogeneous solutions y₁=cos x, y₂=sin x.
u₁′=−sin x sec x=−tan x, u₂′=cos x sec x=1.
y<sub>p</sub>=cos x ln|cos x|+x sin x.

bank.q: Solve the simultaneous system x′=y, y′=x with constant coefficients by elimination.
Given that y₁=x² solves x²y″−2y=0, use reduction of order to find a second independent solution.
outline: Use y₂=y₁∫e<sup>−∫p dx</sup>/y₁² dx with p=0.

bank.q: For x′=x−y, y′=2x−y, find the critical point, Jacobian eigenvalues, and classify the phase portrait.
outline: Critical point solves x−y=0 and 2x−y=0, so (0,0).
Critical point is a centre; nearby paths are closed curves.

bank.q: Derive the variation-of-parameters formula for y″+p(x)y′+q(x)y=f(x) and state the conditions needed.
outline: Let y₁,y₂ be independent homogeneous solutions.
Solve with W: u₁′=−y₂f/W, u₂′=y₁f/W; integrate.

bank.q: Compare undetermined coefficients and variation of parameters for scope, assumptions, and work. Use y″+y=e<sup>x</sup> and y″+y=sec x as examples.
outline: Undetermined coefficients needs constant coefficients and a special right-hand side.
Variation of parameters needs two independent homogeneous solutions and works for general f(x).
For e<sup>x</sup>, undetermined coefficients is shorter.
For sec x, variation of parameters is the practical route.

glossary.def: The order of an ODE is the order of the highest derivative present.
An ODE in which the unknown function and its derivatives appear only to the first power and are not multiplied together.
A linear ODE whose right-hand side is zero.
A linear ODE whose right-hand side is a nonzero function of the independent variable.
The polynomial equation obtained by substituting y=e<sup>mx</sup> into a constant-coefficient homogeneous linear ODE.
The general solution of the associated homogeneous equation.
Any one solution of the nonhomogeneous equation, without arbitrary constants.
The determinant W=y₁y₂′−y₂y₁′ used to test independence of two solutions.
A set of linearly independent solutions whose linear combinations give the general homogeneous solution.
A method that guesses a trial particular solution with unknown constants and solves for them by substitution.
A method that lets the constants in the complementary function vary with x to build a particular integral.
A linear ODE whose coefficients are powers of x matching the derivative order, such as ax²y″+bxy′+cy=f(x).
A Cauchy-Euler type equation with px+q in place of x, solved by px+q=e<sup>t</sup>.
A method that uses one known solution to find a second independent solution of a second-order linear ODE.
A system of ODEs whose right-hand sides do not depend explicitly on t.
The xy-plane used to plot solution curves of an autonomous system when t is eliminated.
A point where both components of an autonomous system vanish.
The matrix of first partial derivatives of P and Q, used to linearise an autonomous system near a critical point.
A scalar λ for which Av=λv has a nonzero vector v; here used to classify critical points.
A critical point to which nearby solution curves tend as t→∞.
A critical point from which nearby solution curves move away as t increases.
A critical point with one positive and one negative real eigenvalue; nearby paths approach and then leave.
A critical point with complex eigenvalues and nonzero real part; nearby paths spiral in or out.
A critical point with pure imaginary eigenvalues; nearby paths are closed curves around it.
The case where the right-hand side duplicates a term in the complementary function, forcing an extra factor x<sup>s</sup> in the trial solution.
